notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0189a.stoa003.opp-l: The edition's source references in parentheses, its footnote marks and its bracketed variants have been left out of the translation; the variants are mala for malefacta, operationem suam for opera sua, and domus spiritualis (suggested) for domos spirituales. Many scanning errors have been silently corrected. In section 1, the printed 'prohibeamus sollicita' ('forbid anxious things') makes poor sense and is translated as 'illicita' ('what is unlawful'), which fits the contrast with 'sequenda'. Also in section 1, 'quem Continui veniens misit' is corrupt and is translated as 'Dominus' ('the Lord'), which suits the allusion to Luke 12:49. 'Nec cui liceat' is taken as 'nec cuiquam liceat'. In section 2, 'animalis' renders the biblical sense of 'unspiritual' or 'merely natural'; 'populus acquisitionis' means a people acquired as God's own possession; 'rationabile lac' is literally 'rational milk'.

Bracketed source citations, footnote marks and the edition's variant readings have been left out, following the practice of the earlier stretches. Variants omitted: 'religiosi' after 'ac' (a good prince and religious king); 'concussas vel conscissas' for 'scissas'; 'justum' for 'juste'; 'opera ejus' for 'ejus opus'; 'congere' for 'congregas'; 'coronabitur' (will be crowned) for 'corroborabitur'. At 'non commovebitur' the edition gives the alternative 'intellexit comparatus est jumentis, et silebitur', apparently a variant or conflation in the Psalm. 'OMnesque exhortareris Me! documenta' is corrupt: 'fidei documenta' (teachings of the faith) is conjectured, though 'Dei' is also possible. 'mellis' is read as 'melius'. 'mutabilem te praeberes' is rendered as it stands, 'showed yourself capable of change'; the sense seems to be that Maxentius should change first. 'ad intentum' makes little sense against 'ne pereamus'; 'ad interitum' (unto destruction) is conjectured. 'Quid gloriaris, qui potens misericordia Dei tota die?' seems to lack words found in the Psalm ('in malitia ... es') and is punctuated here to give sense. 'imponent' is translated as printed; Sirach has the singular 'imponet'. 'suspicio accusantium' is obscure: it may mean the suspicion attaching to the accusers, or their own suspicions.

Several scanning errors have been read as evident: 'at si' as 'ut si', 'ulterias' as 'ulterius', and 'salis' as 'satis'. '15 anno' is taken as the fifteenth year of age, which the text implies but does not state. 'Pœnitendi locum' could also mean 'opportunity for repentance', but in context it appears to refer to going back on the decision.

nodes.text: OF POPE MARCELLUS TO THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF ANTIOCH.
On the primacy and authority of the Roman Church, etc.
To his most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout the province of Antioch, Marcellus.

Carrying about, as the Apostle says, the care of all the churches, we ought to be mindful of the divine grace toward us, [grace] which through the mercy of his condescension advanced us to the height of the priesthood for this purpose: that, holding fast to his commandments and set in a kind of watchtower of his priesthood, we should forbid what is unlawful and teach what is to be followed. Therefore, by a letter sent through our deacon Boniface, we admonish that the things that sprout up evilly be cut away, that misdeeds be corrected, that good things be pursued, and that the examples and statutes of our fathers be imitated. We therefore ask you, brothers, not to teach or think anything other than what you have received from the blessed apostle Peter and from the other apostles and fathers. For you were first instructed by him: therefore you ought not to abandon your own father and follow others. For he is the head of the whole Church, to whom the Lord said: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the rest. For his see was at first among you, and afterward, at the Lord's command, it was transferred to Rome, over which, with divine grace assisting, we preside on this present day. Nor ought you to stray from the ordering of this see, to which all the greater ecclesiastical matters (by the disposition of divine grace) have been commanded to be referred, so that they may be settled according to rule by that [see] from which they took their beginnings. And if your own [see] of Antioch, which was once first, gave way to the Roman see, there is none that is not subject to its dominion. To it, as to the head, according to the sanctions of the apostles and their successors, all bishops who wish to or who have need ought to flee for refuge and to appeal to it, so as to receive protection and deliverance from the place from which they received instruction and consecration. This is by no means fitting to deny to any bishops; rather, let them be allowed to go freely, without any custody, or excommunication, or condemnation, or despoiling. At the same time they likewise decreed (by the Lord's inspiration) that no synod should be held apart from the authority of this same see, and that no bishop, when accused of any crimes whatever, should be heard or judged except in a lawful synod convened at its proper time by apostolic authority; because (as was touched on a little above) the judgments of bishops, and the business of the highest cases, and all doubtful matters, are to be conducted and concluded by the authority of the apostolic see. And all provincial business is to be reconsidered by the judgment of this holy, universal and apostolic Church, if the pontiff of this Church so orders. Nor is anyone permitted, without prejudice to the Roman Church (to which reverence ought to be preserved in all cases), to leave the priests who by divine will govern the churches of God in the same province, and to hasten away to other provinces, or to seek or undergo the judgment of the bishops of other provinces; rather, when all the bishops of the same province have been assembled, let the judgment be concluded by the authority of this see. This, however (as was said before), shall be dealt with through its vicars, if it so pleases, and whatever has been done unjustly shall be set right. The care of the pastoral office therefore admonishes us both to help the destitute and to set right all that has been neglected or badly done, so that that fire which the Lord at his coming sent upon the earth, stirred by the frequent motion of correction or of frequent meditation, may so grow warm as to burn hot, and may so be kindled as to give light.

For it must often be said and done, because evils as they sprout up ought to be cut back by brotherly charity, so that good things may find the fullest room to grow and increase. Therefore (as the apostle James says), do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you incur a greater judgment. For in many things we all offend. If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man: he is able also to lead the whole body about with a bridle. And if we put bridles into the mouths of horses to make them comply with us, we turn their whole body about as well. See also the ships: though they are great and are driven by strong winds, yet they are turned about by a small rudder wherever the impulse of the one steering wills. So too the tongue is a small member indeed, and it exalts great things. See how great a fire, how great a forest it sets ablaze. And the tongue is a fire; the tongue is set among our members as the whole of iniquity, which stains the whole body and sets on fire the wheel of our birth, being set on fire by Gehenna. For all natures of beasts and birds and serpents, and of the rest also, are tamed and have been tamed by human nature. But the tongue no human being can tame. [It is] a restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing. These things ought not to be so, my brothers. Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening? Can a fig tree, my brothers, produce olives, or a vine figs? So neither can salt [water] produce sweet water. Who is wise and disciplined among you? Let him show by good conduct his works in the gentleness of wisdom. But if you have bitter zeal, and there are contentions in your hearts, do not boast and be liars against the truth. For this is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but earthly, animal and diabolical. For where there is zeal and contention, there is instability and every evil work. But the wisdom that is from above is first of all chaste, then peaceable, modest, open to persuasion, agreeing with good things, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without pretence. And the fruit of justice is sown in peace for those who make peace. For this reason, with the loins of your mind girded, sober, perfect, hope in the grace that is offered to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ, as children of obedience, not conformed to the former desires of your ignorance, but according to him who called you, the holy one, so that you yourselves may also be holy in all conduct, since it is written: You shall be holy, because I am holy. And if you call on him as father who judges without regard for persons according to the work of each, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourning, knowing that you were redeemed from your vain way of life inherited from your fathers not with corruptible gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Jesus Christ, as of an undefiled and spotless Lamb, foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world, but made manifest in the last times for your sake, who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that our faith and hope might be in God: purifying your souls in the obedience of charity, in the love of brotherhood, love one another more earnestly from a simple heart, reborn not from corruptible seed but from incorruptible, through the word of the living and abiding God: because all flesh is as grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. The grass has withered, and its flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord abides for ever. And this is the word that has been preached as gospel among you. Putting aside, then, all malice and all deceit, and pretences, and envies, and all slanders, like newborn infants long for the rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow to salvation: if indeed you taste that the Lord is sweet. Coming to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honoured by God, you yourselves also, as living stones, are being built up as spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. For this reason Scripture contains: See, I lay in Zion a chief stone, a cornerstone, chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. To you who believe, therefore, [there is] honour; but to those who do not believe, the stone that the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, to those who stumble at the word and do not believe, to which they also were appointed. But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. Be prudent, therefore, dearest ones, and keep watch in prayers. But before all things have constant mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins. [Be] hospitable to one another without murmuring, each one, as he has received grace, administering it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, [let it be] as words of God; if anyone serves, as from the strength that God supplies, that in all things God may be honoured through Jesus Christ, to whom is glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen. Given on the kalends of April, in the consulship of Maxentius and Maximus, most distinguished men.
OF POPE MARCELLUS I TO THE TYRANT MAXENTIUS.
He admonishes the tyrant to stop raging against the Christians.
Marcellus, bishop of the holy, apostolic and catholic city of Rome, to Maxentius.

Charity, the teacher of all good things, which seizes nothing belonging to another, does nothing harsh, nothing confused, nothing factious, nothing that is opposed to divine honour, harms one's own soul, or detracts from a neighbour's advantage; which, forgetful of itself, seeks not its own things but those of God and of a neighbour, envying no one, caring for all, not raging but feeling compassion, not seizing but giving freely, not murmuring but bearing all things with an even mind: if this dwelt perfectly in you, you would restrain your mind from evils, you would stop raging, you would cease to persecute the Church of God and his saints, you would set a limit to your tyranny, you would hold back your fury, you would attend to humanity, you would embrace moderation, and you would busy yourself to enjoy better goods. For charity exercises hearts and strengthens the senses, so that nothing is burdensome, nothing difficult, but all that is done becomes sweet, since it is its proper work to nurture peaceful things, to preserve what is well ordered, to join what has been separated, to straighten what is crooked, and to make the other virtues firm with the protection of its own perfection. Concerning it, therefore, the Apostle, admonishing all, speaks thus, saying: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a tinkling cymbal. And if I have all prophecy, and know all mysteries, and all knowledge, and have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my means as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing. Charity is patient, it is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own things, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails. Whoever, therefore, grafts himself into its root neither loses his greenness nor grows empty of fruits, because through love of fruitfulness he does not lose effective work. Although charity has now withered in the persecutors of the Church and of the servants of God, it nevertheless flourishes in those who love it, and in those who suffer for the sake of justice. Concerning these the Truth himself testifies, saying: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice. And elsewhere: If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you. For we and all the priests of the Lord, those, that is, who are his true priests, choose rather to be persecuted for the sake of justice and the true faith, and to suffer for the name of Christ, than to be enriched with many riches and to abound in the most copious honours, and to lack the heavenly kingdom. For these things are temporal, those eternal; these are perishable and pass away within the hour, but those are perpetual and will remain without end. You, then, who urge us to abandon divine worship, and to withdraw from the right faith, and to sacrifice to the gods: it would be better for you if you first showed yourself capable of change, and exhorted all to hold the teachings of [the faith] and the ministries of divine worship just as our fathers the holy apostles preached and taught what had been handed down to them. For it is the part of a good prince and king to restore churches that have been crushed and torn apart, to build new ones, and to honour and protect the priests of God. Hence we read that the holy apostles and their successors established, under solemn divine charge, that persecutions must not take place, nor disturbances be inflicted, nor those labouring in the Lord's field be envied, nor the stewards of the eternal King be expelled; but that, if any have been expelled or despoiled of their property, first everything that was taken from them by enemies or persecutors should be lawfully returned, and their own sees, with all that belongs to them, should be restored according to the rule, and afterwards, at a suitable time, they should be summoned to a synod assembled according to the rule. Nor, before these things are done, is he permitted, according to the statutes of those aforesaid, to answer concerning himself, or to render an account of the charges against him, if he sees that he is being oppressed. But when these things have been duly completed, and all his affairs freely arranged, then, if it seems just, let him answer his accusers, and let him receive, if he needs it, a delay of no small length, so that he may be able to examine what is charged against him, lest, deceived by some fraud, he should fall though innocent; since no one ought to be judged or condemned before he has his lawful accusers present and receives an opportunity of defending himself, to wash away the charges. Hence the prophet says: Before you know, do not judge anyone. In this, therefore, that bishops and the other servants of God suffer persecution, it is not so much they themselves who suffer persecution as he in whose stead they act, as it is written: He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye. And elsewhere: He who has grieved you has grieved me. And he who does injury will receive back what he has wickedly done. You, then, though you can kill our bodies, nevertheless cannot kill our souls; nor can you take away from us the ranks divinely conferred on us. Therefore, without the authority of this holy see you cannot hold a synod of bishops according to the rule (although you may be able to assemble certain bishops), nor condemn any bishop who has appealed to this apostolic see, before a final sentence proceeds from here. For if laymen use written appeals in public courts, how much more are the priests, who are above them, permitted to do the same? Of whom it has been said: I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. And therefore let no bishop, accused of any crimes whatever, be heard or judged except in a lawful synod, at its proper time, convened by apostolic or regular authority, lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. That laymen or suspect persons ought not to accuse bishops, and that accusers coming from an enemy's house are not to be believed, we read was also laid down by the blessed Clement, the apostles themselves instructing him, and we confirm the same: since these same people, often hostile, now strive to disturb those who live and believe rightly. For this reason the person, faith, life and conduct, and the suspicion [attaching to] the accusers must first be carefully investigated; then what is charged must be faithfully examined, because nothing ought to be done before the life, suspicion and hatred of the accusers are investigated. And if they are not of good conduct, or are laymen, or open enemies, or are tainted with hatred, let them by no means be admitted in an accusation of bishops. These things we command to be made known to you, by whom we are so very bitterly persecuted, so that you may beware of them and cease to persecute those who minister to God, by whose prayers both earthly wars are quelled and God is reconciled to sinners. And if you choose rather to persecute us than to please God, we too choose rather to endure persecution than to have the ecclesiastical rule thrown into confusion, the very voice of truth exhorting us and testifying thus: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. And again: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For he who wishes to save his life will lose it. But he who loses his life for my sake will find it. For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul? For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each one according to his work. These things are greatly to be feared and guarded against by you, by whom the Church of God and his ministers are harassed and suffer persecution, to whom the Lord speaks threateningly through the prophet, saying: Man will not remain in honour: he is likened to the beasts, made equal to them. This is their way, their folly, and after them they will run according to their mouth. Like sheep they are placed in hell; death will feed on them. And the upright will subdue them in the morning, and their form will be worn away in hell after their dwelling. Yet God will redeem my soul from the hand of hell, when he takes me up. Do not fear when a man has become rich, when the glory of his house has been multiplied. For in dying he will not take everything away, nor will his glory go down after him. For he will bless his soul in his life. They will praise you when it goes well with you. He will enter even to the generation of his fathers; he will not see light to the end. Man, when he was in honour, will not be moved: he is likened to the beasts, made equal to them. And elsewhere: Why do you boast, you who are powerful? The mercy of God [endures] all day. Your tongue has devised plots, working deceit like a sharp razor. You have loved evil more than good, falsehood more than speaking justice. You have loved all words for devouring, deceitful tongue. But God will destroy you for ever, he will terrify you, and tear you from your tent, and root you out of the land of the living. And the just will see and will fear, and they will laugh over him: Behold the man who did not make God his strength, but hoped in the abundance of his riches, and was strengthened in his plots. But I, like a living olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God for the age and for eternity. I will praise you for the age, because you have acted, and I will wait for your name, because it is good in the sight of your saints. All these things have been said for you unto [destruction], but for us for comfort, that we may not perish. We therefore write these things to you because we are your debtors, as the Lord says: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you. And elsewhere Scripture speaks, saying: If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For in doing this you gather coals of fire upon his head. Supported by these authorities, we desire to bear peacefully the war that you stir up against us, the right hand of the Lord so happily protecting us and fighting for us, that with Christ triumphant there may be one victory of all true priests, and that, with the light of truth flashing, the darkness of error alone may be driven out together with its authors: because the counsel of God is not in man's power. For the Lord is just, and all his judgments are just, and all his ways are mercy and truth and judgment. In the hand of God is the power over the earth, and to him all iniquity is abominable. In the hand of God is the power over man, and upon the face of the scribe they will place his honour. God has destroyed the memory of the proud and of those who act wickedly, and has not abandoned the memory of the humble and of good men. But everyone who rightly worships God holds this for certain: that if his life is under trial, he will be strengthened; and if in tribulation, he will be delivered; and if he is under correction, he will come to mercy. Do not, then, delight in our ruin, because after the storm God brings calm, and after weeping and lamentation he pours in rejoicing. Blessed be the Lord God of our fathers, who, when he has been angry, will show mercy, and in the time of tribulation forgives sins. Great is the Lord for ever, and he will rule us for ages, for his kingdom endures for ages of ages. Amen. Given on the sixteenth day before the kalends of February, in the consulship of Maxentius and Maximus, most distinguished men.
Those shut away in monasteries against their own will are not to be held there.

We judge that this also must be established: that if children have been offered to a monastery while under age, or have received the sacred tonsure or the veil, we have indeed thought it right that in [their] fifteenth year they be admonished by their superiors and questioned in words whether they wish to remain in that habit or not. If they declare that they will remain, they can by no means take up any further opportunity for changing their minds. But if they wish to return to secular dress, permission to go back is in no way to be refused, because service rendered to the Lord under compulsion is quite useless.
